learningObjective: Contrast tensor-typed IR (value semantics) with buffer-/memref-typed IR (reference semantics) and explain what bufferization does.

canonicalClaims.claim: In MLIR, tensor-typed IR has value semantics — each op produces a fresh, immutable SSA value — while memref-typed IR has reference semantics — ops write into named buffers. Bufferization lowers tensor form to memref form, assigning buffers and inserting allocations/copies to preserve the tensor-level dataflow.
conditions: Standard MLIR type system (tensor + memref dialects).
Bufferization is configured to preserve semantics (with copies when required).
nonImplications: Does not imply bufferization always eliminates copies; unavoidable copies are inserted where alias-safety cannot be proven.
Does not imply memref form is always closer to codegen; some pipelines lower tensor form directly.

misconceptions.claim: Tensor-typed IR has reference semantics; memref has value semantics.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The relationship is reversed; tensor SSA values are immutable.

misconceptions.claim: Tensor and memref forms are textually distinct but semantically identical.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The data model differs: value vs. reference semantics affect what optimizations are safe.

misconceptions.claim: Bufferization only removes duplicated tensor ops (i.e., a form of CSE).
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bufferization assigns buffers and manages allocations/copies; CSE is a separate pass.

misconceptions.claim: Bufferization chooses between GPU and CPU codegen based on the tensor form.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Device selection is a separate concern (target dialects, launch, backends); bufferization is target-independent.

implementationFacts: MLIR tensor SSA values are immutable; each producing op yields a new tensor
MLIR memref values reference underlying buffers; multiple ops can update the same memref
Bufferization assigns buffers and may insert copies when the tensor-level dataflow requires it
performanceScenarios: Well-implemented bufferization reduces allocations and copies substantially; when it fails, generated code carries extra memory traffic.
